Jedwabne Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Jedwabne, Poland

Not demolished. Jedwabne's Jewish population reached 1,410 (75.9 percent of the town) in 1880. On July 10, 1941, a group of Poles, assisted by the Germans, carried out a pogrom in which several hundred Jews were burned alive in a barn next to this cemetery, with others killed in the town and surrounding area — one of the most documented and historically significant pogroms of the Holocaust in Poland. This cemetery, likely established in the second half of the 18th century, was first mentioned in an inspection record of the local Catholic parish in 1781. In June 1941, the Germans used the cemetery as a defensive base, and in 1944 dug trenches there to defend against the advancing Red Army, with a battle fought on the site on January 23, 1945. In 2001, as part of a project commemorating the pogrom's victims, a stone wall and informational monument were erected at the cemetery.
